source: Varambally, Voice, Sun, Chen, Yu, Ye (2026, ICLR) Hilbert: recursively building formal proofs with informal reasoning
finding: A code-owned loop around off-the-shelf models: a general informal reasoner, a Lean prover, a formal verifier and a retriever. If the prover fails, the reasoner splits the goal into subgoals, the prover or reasoner solves each, and failures are split again up to depth D. Verifier errors are fed back for repair. Large gains over the prover alone at pass@4.
numbers: miniF2F-test (244): Gemini 2.5 Pro + Goedel-Prover-V2-32B 99.2% (+24.6 over the pass@4 prover at 74.6%); Gemini 2.5 Flash + same prover 94.7% (+20.1); gpt-oss-120b + same prover 90.8% (+16.2). With DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B non-CoT (61.3% at pass@4): Pro 98.4% (+37.1), Flash 96.7% (+35.4). PutnamBench (660): 462 solved = 70.0% with Gemini 2.5 Pro; gpt-oss-120b 88/660 = 13.3%. For comparison Seed-Prover 50.4% and best public baseline 86/644 = 13.4%.
quote: Compared to standalone base provers at pass@4, our approach delivers substantial improvements ranging from 16.2% to 37.1%.
limits: The prover and verifier models were trained by others; the loop itself is not trained. The headline PutnamBench number used exhaustive retries with no compute tracking. Baselines are pass@4 (a few thousand tokens) against a recursive loop averaging hundreds of calls, so it is not an equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 6: recursive decomposition into checked subgoals plus feedback repair, orchestrated by code around off-the-shelf models, beats a monolithic attempt by a large margin. Not equal-token though.

source: Hilbert ablations: recursion depth and retrieval
finding: Decomposition depth gives most of the gain by depth 2. Retrieval of library theorems raises pass rate and cuts compute.
numbers: Depth D=0 (no decomposition, prover pass@4) about 75%; full system 98.36% at D=2 and 98.7% at D=3; the no-shallow-solve variant needs more depth. Retrieval: DS-Prover-V2-7B 98.4% vs 97.1% without; Goedel-V2-32B 99.2% vs 97.9%. Goedel case: average reasoner calls 862 to 548, average reasoner tokens 4.0M to 2.3M per sample (over samples needing decomposition).
limits: One benchmark (miniF2F). Differences of about 1 point are 2 to 3 problems of 244. Depth ablation compares to pass@4, not to a pass@N at matched calls.
agent_relevance: Marginal return of recursion falls fast after depth 2: a depth cap of 2 to 3 is enough in S3. Retrieval helps by avoiding wrong lemma names.

source: Hilbert inference-time compute (Fig. 3, Tables 4-5, App. A.6)
finding: Pass rate climbs steadily with calls and tokens. The informal reasoner, not the prover, drives the result. Compute has a long tail: a few hard problems eat most of the budget.
numbers: miniF2F: best config needs at most 4.5K reasoner calls and 11.3K total calls per sample, vs Delta Prover 16,384 calls with Gemini 2.5 Pro (95.9%); hardest problems used 22.8M and 27.0M tokens. PutnamBench re-run with strictly one attempt per problem: Gemini 2.5 Pro 55.9% (vs 70.0% exhaustive), gpt-oss-120b 13.3% (unchanged). Average tokens per solved Putnam problem 24.4M (Gemini) vs 2.0M (gpt-oss); median LLM calls 817 vs mean 5352. The paper says Pro beats Flash by 3-4 points; the table gap is 1.7 to 4.5.
quote: Notably, the choice of informal reasoner appears more critical than prover strength.
limits: Calls are not tokens; the call-count comparison with Delta Prover is not token-matched. No pass@N baseline at 11.3K calls was run for the same model pair.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a weaker model (gpt-oss-120b) gets 13.3% where a stronger one gets 55.9% from the same loop. The loop multiplies capability; it does not create it. Budgets reach 24M tokens per problem, far past a context window, which only a code-owned loop can carry.

source: Ren, Shao, Song et al. (2025) DeepSeek-Prover-V2: RL for subgoal decomposition
finding: A general model (DeepSeek-V3) writes a lemma-style sketch with sorry gaps; a small 7B prover fills each subgoal recursively; solved sketches become chain-of-thought training data. The decomposition pipeline alone nearly matches the 671B prover on the validation set.
numbers: miniF2F-test 82.4% at pass@32 and 88.9% at pass@8192 (671B). miniF2F-valid 90.6% for 671B vs 89.8% for the 7B-prover plus V3-decomposition pipeline. PutnamBench 47 of 658. Average output tokens per sample non-CoT vs CoT: 7B 442.6 vs 4488.5; 671B 761.8 vs 6751.9.
limits: Trained: decomposition data feeds RL. The valid-set pipeline number is on the set used to build training data, not a clean test. The paper uses a revised miniF2F with extra fixes.
agent_relevance: Supports K16 with a small-executor result: general planner plus cheap executor is near the large prover. Needs a frozen-model replication (Hilbert, LEGO-Prover).

source: Wang, Xin, Zheng et al. (2023) LEGO-Prover: neural theorem proving with growing libraries
finding: A frozen ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), no fine-tuning: informal proof, decomposer turns it into a lemma-style sketch, prover fills, and verified lemmas are stored in a skill library for later problems. Library growth is the ablated component.
numbers: Isabelle miniF2F: 57.0% valid / 50.0% test at 100 attempts vs Thor 42.6 / 39.3, Thor + expert iteration 48.0 / 45.5, subgoal-learning 52.4 / 45.5. Ablation at 50 attempts on valid: 50.4% with library vs 47.1% without (+3.3 points, about 8 problems of 244). Skill origins: 10.8% prover, 38.2% evolver solve-requests, 51.1% evolver transformations. 24% of verified valid proofs used retrieved skills.
limits: Same ChatGPT for all roles; per-attempt cost is higher than a plain sample and not matched to baselines. Ablation only at 50 attempts. Informal proofs came from GPT-4 (possible indirect contamination).
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for gap 6 with no training: decomposition plus verified-lemma reuse helps a frozen model. A growing store of checked lemmas is a persistent working memory. The library alone adds only about 3 points.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Seed-Prover: deep and broad reasoning for automated theorem proving
finding: Three test-time tiers: light (refine a whole proof 8 to 16 times on Lean errors with self-summary), medium (outer refinement plus inner refinement of failed lemmas), heavy (thousands of conjectures, prove or refute, keep lemmas). The paper claims refinement beats raw pass@k but gives no matched ablation.
numbers: Light budget stated as equivalent to whole-proof Pass@64 to 256 (n x m refinements), 1 to 2 hours. IMO 2022 P2 proved in light setting, otherwise only at Pass@8192. miniF2F-test 99.6%, miniF2F-valid 100%, PutnamBench 331/657, past IMO 78.1% (heavy), IMO 2025 4/6 in competition, 5/6 after.
quote: iteratively refining proofs using Lean compiler feedback ... can surpass the limits of single-pass inference token budgets
limits: 'Equivalent to Pass@64-256' counts attempts, not tokens; refined attempts carry long histories. One problem anecdote (IMO 2022 P2) is the only paired comparison. No light-versus-resample curve is shown. Model is RL-trained and closed.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 stays open: the refinement-vs-resampling advantage is asserted, not measured at equal tokens.

source: Li and Li (2026, NeurIPS) Repair, Retry, and the Cost of Hindsight: verifier feedback in formal theorem proving
finding: Controlled one-step experiments on hard miniF2F problems with Qwen3.6-27B (general) and DeepSeek-Prover-V2-7B. Showing the model its own failed proof lowers success; adding the compiler error recovers part of the loss on Qwen; correct diagnostics beat wrong ones only when the failed proof is shown; no tested feedback condition beats instruction-only resampling.
numbers: Sequential experiment: 11 problems, 64 attempts. Qwen keeps a correct-diagnostic benefit inside failed-proof histories; DeepSeek-Prover shows none. The failed-proof penalty comes with sharply increased copying of the failed proof. Swapping in another theorem's failed proof removes most of the degradation. No pass-rate table on the page.
quote: No tested one-step condition beats instruction-only resampling, and neither does sequential repair at 64 attempts.
limits: Only the NeurIPS abstract page was read (no arXiv full text found, OpenReview not opened); no numeric rates available. Small sample (11 problems), two models, hard problems with low base rates. Whether attempts were token-matched is not stated.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct counter-evidence for gap 2: feeding back a failed attempt can hurt through anchoring, and fresh resampling is the fair baseline. In our schema a retry should pass only the diagnostic, not the failed text, and be tested against plain resampling.

source: Mahdavi, Kisacanin, Toshniwal et al. (2025, NVIDIA) Scaling generative verifiers for natural-language proof verification and selection
finding: LLM judges of natural-language proofs look accurate but can be gamed by shallow cues. A trivial classifier matches mid LLM judges. The strongest judge still passes wrong proofs when correct ones are rare, and majority voting did not fix it.
numbers: Two-layer MLP on Qwen3-0.6B embeddings scored 75.34% on the OPC test set, more than 5 points above Claude-Sonnet-4. A keyword rule ('triangle' etc.) scored 65.07%, above Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1. GPT-5 (high thinking) judging GPT-OSS proofs on USAMO 2025 problems 5 and 6: 48 candidate proofs, 7 judged correct although all 7 had critical errors; accuracy 41/48 = 87.2%; a ground-truth solution in the prompt or majority of 5 judgements did not fix it. Judge scaling saturates at about 32 judgements per proof. GenSelect tournament vs LLM-as-judge: no clear winner. Datasets: VerOPC 204 proofs, VerProofBench 429, SelProofBench only 29 problems x 16 proofs.
quote: it cannot be fully trusted to reliably judge mathematical proofs, especially when the correct proofs are rare
limits: The 7-of-48 test is one judge on two problems. Datasets are small; 3.44 points on SelProofBench is one problem. Human labels may be noisy.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the strongest judge false-passed 7 of 48 hard flawed proofs (about 15%), and extra votes or a reference solution did not help. Under G2 an LLM verifier is advisory, never the final gate.

source: Gonzalez, Amiri Bavandpour, Ye et al. (2026, ICML) QEDBench: alignment gap in automated evaluation of university-level proofs
finding: 272 expert-graded proof problems (upper undergraduate to early graduate, 1,000+ human hours). LLM judges differ widely in leniency: some pass most flawed proofs, others reject valid ones.
numbers: Human pass rate 67.7% (score >= 0.9). Llama 4 Maverick as judge: 90.2% pass rate, 74.8% leniency rate (false positives). GPT-5.2 Pro: pass rate 74.1%, leniency 38.0% even as the best judge. DeepSeek-V3: pass 72.2% (closest to human), leniency 39.6%, harshness (false negatives) 12.3%. The paper cites Jain et al. 2025: judges accept correct solutions at TPR above 96% but reject invalid ones at TNR below 25% (second-hand, not opened).
quote: approving nearly three-quarters of logically flawed proofs
limits: University-level proofs, not olympiad; rubrics and labels come from the authors' own experts; judge versions are as of 2026.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: independent confirmation that LLM judges are lenient: false-pass rates 38% to 75% on flawed proofs, false rejects at most 12%. Leniency is the dominant failure and the dangerous direction for a verifier gate.

source: Naik, Shabadi, Alur, Naik (2026) Do we need frontier models to verify mathematical proofs?
finding: Six LLM judges on three human-graded olympiad proof sets (IMO-GradingBench, ProofArena, ProofBench): balanced accuracy 77 to 88%, self-consistency (same verdict on three identical queries) much lower for small models, and accuracy depends heavily on the prompt. An LLM-searched prompt ensemble lifts small judges to frontier level.
numbers: Balanced accuracy 76.6% (Qwen3.5-35B) to 87.7% (Gemini 3.1 Pro, low reasoning). Small models up to 10 points behind in accuracy and up to 25 points less self-consistent; the GIMO prompt dropped GPT-5.2 (high) balanced accuracy by 27.3 points (it rejects correct proofs). Prompt ensemble: up to +9.1 accuracy and +15.9 self-consistency. Correct = score 7 only. TrainProofs set: 140 incorrect and 60 correct proofs.
limits: The text calls higher false-negative rates 'a greater tendency to accept flawed proofs', which contradicts its own metric definition; read the figure before relying on direction. Labels are binarised from 0-7 scores.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: even the best judge is wrong on about 1 proof in 8, small judges flip verdicts across identical re-queries, and the prompt moves accuracy by up to 27 points. A verifier prompt must be tested, and repeated judgements need agreement before acceptance.

source: Jiang, Li, Tworkowski et al. (2022) Thor: wielding hammers (ablations re-read)
finding: Thor trains the model to emit a <hammer> token meaning 'call Sledgehammer here', learning only when to call the solver. A plain union of model alone and solver alone does worse than the interleaved loop. No test of a fixed always-call-first rule at every state.
numbers: PISA/test (3,000 theorems): language model 39.0%, Sledgehammer 25.7% (120 s), union 48.8%, Thor 57.0% (interleaving adds 8.2 over the union). Variants: model also learns how to pick premises 55.4% (-1.6); no proof context 53.6% (-3.4); temperature 1.0 55.7% (-1.3). miniF2F test: Sledgehammer 10.4, model 24.2, model + Sledgehammer 27.5, Thor 29.9 (valid 9.9 / 25.0 / 27.1 / 28.3).
limits: The baseline is a union of independent runs, not a rule like 'try the solver at every goal before asking the model'. Gap 9 (learned vs fixed rule) is therefore not answered. Isabelle only; small miniF2F differences are 1 to 2 problems.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open. Evidence says call the solver inside the loop at states, not once at the end. 'Try solver at every new goal, then ask the model' is the untested cheap alternative and easy to test.

source: Xin et al. (2025) BFS-Prover: scalable best-first tree search (score design re-read)
finding: Best-first search with a priority queue where node score = sum of tactic log-probabilities divided by path length to the power alpha (alpha in 0..1). The score comes from the model's own probabilities, not a learned critic and not code-computed goal features. No critic, no MCTS.
numbers: miniF2F-test 70.83% +/- 0.89 at pass 2048 x expansion 2 x 600 tactic budget; 72.95% accumulative over alpha in {0.0, 0.5, 1.0}; default alpha 0.5, width 2, temperature 1.1. SFT+DPO 64.98% at pass@64 to 70.83% at pass@2048. A critic roughly doubles inference calls per expansion (paper). Listed rivals: InternLM2.5-StepProver 65.9% with critic (256x32x600), HunyuanProver 68.4% with critic (600x8x400), DeepSeek-Prover-V1.5 63.5% with MCTS (32x16x400).
limits: No matched ablation of critic vs no critic; rivals differ in model and budget. Per-alpha results not reported. The score is policy likelihood, so it says nothing about code-computed state scores (open goals, size).
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays mostly open: a no-learned-value best-first search is competitive, which supports a cheap score, but nobody has run an open-goal-count score head to head against a value head. Length normalisation is the one tuned knob.

source: Cao, Song, Li et al. (2025, Microsoft) Reviving DSP for advanced theorem proving in the era of reasoning models (DSP+)
finding: Training-free rebuild of Draft-Sketch-Prove in Lean 4 from off-the-shelf models (QwQ-32B draft, DeepSeek-V3-0324 sketch, BFS-Prover tactic prover, Aesop symbolic search). Matches heavily trained provers at lower token cost. Earlier Lean re-implementations had been weak.
numbers: miniF2F-test 79.5% at 1024 workflow attempts (80.7% with DeepSeek-R1 as drafter); ProofNet-test 32.8% at 128; PutnamBench 24/644 at 128; ensemble accumulative 83.6% / 33.9% / 25/644; miniF2F/IMO 40 to 45%. Prior Lean re-implementations of DSP reached at most 28% and 31% of miniF2F (cited), blamed on Aesop being weaker than Sledgehammer. Found 8 wrongly formalised miniF2F statements. Claims fewer total inference tokens than Kimina-Prover-Preview-72B.
limits: Token comparisons use numbers taken from other papers, with different Lean versions (a note says Lean v4.9 issues may hurt DeepSeek-Prover-V2). Ensemble accumulative is a union over configurations. The step prover BFS-Prover is trained.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 (replication in Lean with current LLMs): yes, the scaffold works without training, but see d14 on how little the informal draft adds. Also a scaffold that exposes benchmark errors.

source: DSP+ ablations: what the informal draft and the prover each add
finding: With a strong step prover, the informal draft adds little. Drafts from reasoning models help a few points; no draft is as good as GPT-4o's. Human-written informal proofs gave no overall gain, unlike original DSP. The proving tools matter most.
numbers: miniF2F-test at pass@128 by draft model: none 71.7%, GPT-4o 71.7%, DeepSeek-V3 73.0%, QwQ-32B 74.2%, DeepSeek-R1 75.8% (figure legends, default prover). Proving phase: BFS-Prover 74.2% vs common tactics only 47.5%. Removing hypothesis specification or error-line masking in the sketch causes a significant drop and lower sample efficiency. Removing conciseness prompting slightly raised accuracy at larger pass@k.
quote: incorporating informal proofs does not lead to an overall improvement in performance, which is different from the original DSP
limits: Values read from figure legends; single benchmark; differences of 1 to 2 points are 2 to 5 problems. Pass@128 workflow attempts, not equal tokens.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: DSP's headline (model-written draft about equal to human draft) holds, and a stronger point appears: with a good executor the draft adds only about 0 to 4 points, so most gain is in code-checked execution of subgoals (S3, S4), not the plan text. Do not spend heavy tokens on the plan.

source: Tsoukalas, Lee, Jennings et al. (2024) PutnamBench: neural theorem-provers on the Putnam competition
finding: 1,712 formalisations (640 Lean, 640 Isabelle, 412 Coq) of Putnam problems. Authors argue the formal statements are new so direct leakage is avoided, but note one indirect route: DSP uses GPT-4 to write informal drafts and informal solutions are public.
numbers: 2024 results: Lean GPT-4 1/640, COPRA 1/640, ReProver 0/640; Isabelle DSP 4/640, Sledgehammer 3/640, GPT-4 1/640; Coq GPT-4 1/412, COPRA 1/412, Tactician 0/412, CoqHammer 0/412. Only problem solved in both Lean and Coq: Putnam 1988 B1. GPT-4 pass@10 at T=0.7; COPRA allowed 60 queries. GPT-4 kept writing Lean 3 syntax in Lean 4.
quote: we cannot ensure the informal proofs are not present in GPT-4's training data
limits: The authors do not measure contamination; they argue by construction. 2025 systems reach 70% (Hilbert) and 331/657 (Seed-Prover) on the same benchmark, from about 0.2% a year earlier; the jump is not explained by the paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: the benchmark is clean only for formal text; informal solutions are public. A test set for our agent should use post-cutoff or restated problems and carry a contamination caveat.

source: Yousefzadeh and Cao (2025) Advocate for complete benchmarks for formal reasoning (position paper)
finding: Position paper. Raises contamination of miniF2F as an unmeasured worry (asks whether authors who report 64% pass@32 on miniF2F-valid after fine-tuning had trained on the validation set) and shows autoformalisation scores can overstate truth.
numbers: An autoformalisation system reported at 97% accuracy by automatic check scored 67% when a Lean expert checked the translations (the authors reproduced the 97%).
limits: A position paper; no contamination measurement. A second-hand review (miniF2F-Lean Revisited, search snippet only, not opened) says over half of miniF2F-v1 statements have formal/informal mismatches and some autoformalisers drop on v2.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: no published measurement of miniF2F or PutnamBench contamination in frontier LLMs was found. What exists is warnings plus benchmark-quality errors (8 wrong statements found by DSP+, 97 vs 67 autoformalisation). Our test set should use fresh items and check the statement as well as the proof (G3).

source: Pythagoras-Prover (2026) five-stage decontamination of miniF2F-test (search snippet only)
finding: Snippet: a 2026 prover paper reports hash, n-gram, embedding and proof-template decontamination against miniF2F-Test and drops training instances with a hit. Not opened; no counts seen.
limits: Search snippet only. Self-reported; removal rate unknown.
agent_relevance: Shows the field treats miniF2F as likely leaked and decontaminates, but gives no leakage rate for general frontier LLMs.

source: Synthesis across opened papers: how strong must the base model be for a scaffold to help
finding: Across loops around frozen models, the gain depends on the strength of the model in the planning role. Weak proposers gain little on hard sets; strong ones multiply their rate.
numbers: Hilbert miniF2F (prover fixed): gpt-oss-120b 90.8%, Flash 94.7%, Pro 99.2%; PutnamBench one attempt: 13.3% vs 55.9% (gpt-oss vs Pro). DS-V2-7B non-CoT pass@4 61.3% becomes 96.7% / 98.4% with Flash / Pro. DSP+ draft: reasoning models 74.2 to 75.8 vs none 71.7 (+2.5 to +4.1). COPRA (earlier): GPT-4 26.63, GPT-3.5 9.02, CodeLlama 5.73. LEGO-Prover on GPT-3.5: 50.0% test. PutnamBench 2024 raw GPT-4 about 0.2% (1/640).
limits: Different benchmarks and budgets; a fixed strong prover in Hilbert and DSP+, so the floor is not isolated. No paper varies the raw pass rate of one model class cleanly. No frontier-model re-run of COPRA was found.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 partly closed: scaffolds help weak models little on hard sets and a lot on medium sets. Rule: measure raw pass rate first; if near zero on the real task, the loop will not rescue it.

source: Tree search vs best-of-N at matched budget: snippets (CS224R project; VG-Search; Snell et al. 2024)
finding: Search results mention a student project where step-level search lost to matched best-of-N (0.613 vs 0.680 and 0.580 vs 0.733), a verification-granularity method with up to +3.6% over best-of-N and 52% fewer FLOPs, and Snell et al. finding PRM search nearly matching best-of-N at 4x less compute. Mixed. None opened.
numbers: Not read; figures from search snippets.
limits: Search snippets only. Informal reasoning tasks with learned verifiers.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 8: outside formal proof the matched-token advantage of search over best-of-N is mixed and verifier-dependent. No paper found that runs a propose-check-backtrack loop against best-of-N at equal tokens in Lean.
